title: "Practical 1: Time Series Objects in R"
format: html
editor: visual
---

This page is my follow-up to the first class practical, which introduced time series objects in R: building a series with `ts()`, cutting it with `window()`, differencing it with `diff()`, and splitting it into a trend and a seasonal part. Here I apply the same tools to real data, the daily closing price of Apple (AAPL) in 2019, taken from the S&P 500 data set I also use in Projects 1 and 2. I build the series twice, once as a base R `ts` object and once as a `tsibble`, to see where the two approaches differ. What I learnt in the practical itself, including the `lag()` and `ts.union()` exercises, is in my [journal entry for Practical 1](../journal/s1-01-fundamentals/2026-08-17-practical-1.qmd).

## Data

```{r data}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tsibble)
library(feasts)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data", "sp500_stocks.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    date   = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    open   = col_double(),
    high   = col_double(),
    low    = col_double(),
    close  = col_double(),
    volume = col_double(),
    symbol = col_character()
  )
)

TICKER <- "AAPL"
YEAR   <- 2019

stock_year <- raw %>%
  filter(symbol == TICKER,
         date >= as.Date(paste0(YEAR, "-01-01")),
         date <= as.Date(paste0(YEAR, "-12-31"))) %>%
  arrange(date)

cat("Rows extracted:", nrow(stock_year), "\n")
cat("Date range:", as.character(min(stock_year$date)), "to",
    as.character(max(stock_year$date)), "\n")
```

The filtered series has 252 rows, from 2 January to 31 December 2019. That is one row per trading day. There are no rows for weekends or public holidays, so a calendar year gives about 252 observations and not 365.

## A base R ts object

```{r ts-object}
# frequency = 252 is the convention for daily trading data
# (not 365, since there are no rows for weekends and holidays)
stock_ts <- ts(stock_year$close, frequency = 252)

plot.ts(stock_ts,
        main = paste(TICKER, YEAR, "- Daily Close (Base R ts)"),
        ylab = "Close Price ($)", xlab = "Time (trading years)",
        col = "darkblue", lwd = 1.5)
abline(h = mean(stock_ts), col = "grey", lty = 2)
```

I stored the closing prices with `frequency = 252`, so one unit on the x axis is one trading year, and the axis runs from 1 to 2 instead of counting days. The price starts the year at about \$37, drops to about \$34 on the second trading day, and ends the year at about \$71, close to double. The rise is not steady. The price climbs to about \$50 by early May, falls back to about \$42 by early June, and then rises for the rest of the year. The dashed line is the mean for the year, about \$50, and the price stays above or below it for months at a time, so the level of the series is not constant.

## window() and diff()

```{r window-diff}
# window(): the last part of the year, roughly the fourth quarter
q4 <- window(stock_ts, start = c(1, 190), end = c(1, 252))
plot.ts(q4, main = paste(TICKER, YEAR, "Q4 (approx, via window())"),
        ylab = "Close Price ($)", xlab = "Time (trading years)")

# diff(): change from one trading day to the next
plot.ts(diff(stock_ts), main = paste(TICKER, "- Day-on-day change"),
        ylab = "Change ($)", xlab = "Time (trading years)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

`window()` cuts out part of a `ts` object by time. Trading day 190 of 252 is roughly the start of the fourth quarter, so the first plot shows the last quarter of 2019, when the price rose from about \$53 to about \$71.

`diff()` gives the change in price from one trading day to the next. The daily changes move around zero and most of them are within about \$1.50 either way. The largest fall, of about \$3.70, is on the second trading day of the year, which is the drop at the start of the price plot. Unlike the price, the changes have no trend, which is why differencing is the usual first step for a series like this.

## A tsibble version

```{r tsibble}
# Index by trading day, not by calendar date: indexed by date, ACF()
# reads weekends and holidays as missing days and stops with an error
stock_tsbl <- stock_year %>%
  select(date, close, symbol) %>%
  mutate(trading_day = row_number()) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = trading_day, key = symbol)

count_gaps(stock_tsbl)

stock_tsbl %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = close)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = paste(TICKER, YEAR, "- Daily Close"),
       y = "Close Price ($)", x = "Date") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b")
```

A `tsibble` needs a regular index. When I first indexed it by calendar date, `ACF()` stopped with an implicit-gaps error, because the weekends and holidays look like missing days. So I index it by trading day, a row number from 1 to 252, and keep the date as an extra column for plotting. `count_gaps()` then returns an empty table, so the trading-day index has no gaps. The plot shows the same series as above, now with months on the x axis, which places the high in early May and the low in early June.

## Autocorrelation

```{r acf}
#| fig-cap: "ACF of the AAPL daily closing price, 2019"
stock_tsbl %>% ACF(close) %>% autoplot()
```

The ACF starts at about 0.98 at lag 1 and falls very slowly, to about 0.58 at lag 24, and every bar is far above the bounds of about ±0.12. Each day's price is close to the price the day before, so the correlation stays high over many lags. This slow decay is the pattern of a series that is not stationary, and it is the reason Project 1 models the changes and the returns and not the price itself.

## STL decomposition

```{r stl}
# STL needs a period: with trading-day data the only regular cycle
# to try is the trading week, so period = 5
stock_tsbl %>%
  model(STL(close ~ season(period = 5))) %>%
  components() %>%
  autoplot()
```

STL splits the series into a trend, a seasonal part and a remainder. With trading-day data the only regular cycle I can try is the trading week, so I set the period to 5. The trend carries almost all of the movement, from about \$35 to about \$70. The weekly part is tiny next to it, mostly within about \$0.30 either way, and its size and shape change through the year, so there is no stable weekly pattern in the price. The remainder is mostly within about \$1 either way. The grey bars on the left mark the same length on every panel, so the bar on the weekly panel is the tallest because that panel covers the smallest range.

## What I took from this

Two things from this practical carried straight into Project 1. Daily trading data has to be indexed by trading day and not by calendar date, both in `ts()` and in a `tsibble`. And a daily price is dominated by its trend, with no weekly pattern worth modelling, so the models are fitted to the changes or the returns instead of the price.
